--- title: "Clustering with k-means" description: "k-means sorts stations into groups by how alike they are, with no labels to learn from. What it minimises, why it starts many times, and how it finds the two kinds of seabed from species counts alone." order: 1 categories: [unsupervised] --- ## Clustering sorts unlabelled stations into groups Many marine datasets come without an answer column. A benthic survey returns grab samples full of animals, and the first question is which kinds of seabed community it covers. A CTD programme returns thousands of profiles, and the question is which water masses they sample. **Clustering** sorts rows into groups so that rows in the same group resemble each other more than rows in other groups, with no labels to learn from. [Types of learning](../01-introduction/types-of-learning.qmd) ran **k-means**, the most widely used clustering method, on temperature, salinity and depth. This page shows what k-means is doing, then gives it a harder table, two dozen species counted at every station, and finds the kinds of seabed in it without ever being told what they are. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea k-means needs one number from you: $k$, the number of groups. It places $k$ centres at random, then repeats two steps: every point joins its nearest centre, and every centre moves to the average of its points. It stops when no point changes group. ::: {.diagram} ![k-means in three steps. Place k centres at random; assign each point to its nearest centre; move each centre to the average of its points. Steps 2 and 3 repeat until no point changes group, and each round lowers the within-cluster sum of squares.](img/k-means-steps.svg){fig-alt="Three cards joined by arrows, each showing the same sixteen points in two loose groups. 1 Place: the points are grey, and two centres, one blue and one orange, sit at random places among them. 2 Assign: each point is coloured by its nearest centre and joined to it by a thin line; a few points of the lower group are blue. 3 Move: each centre has moved from its faded old position, along a short arrow, to the average of its points. An arrow from the third card back to the second reads repeat steps 2 and 3 until no point changes group. A note says each round lowers the within-cluster sum of squares: the squared distance from every point to its own centre, added up."} ::: Each round makes the groups tighter. The quantity that falls is the **within-cluster sum of squares**: take every point's distance to the centre of its own group, square it, and add them all up. Small means every group is compact. Where k-means ends depends on where the centres started, and a poor start can settle on poor groups. So the usual practice is to run it many times from different random starts and keep the run with the smallest sum. R calls the number of starts `nstart`; scikit-learn calls it `n_init`. "Nearest" is ordinary straight-line distance across all the columns at once. As [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd) showed for every method that measures distance, the columns need a common scale first, or the column with the largest numbers decides every group. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it For points $x_i$, groups $C_1,\dots,C_k$ and centres $\mu_j$, k-means minimises $$W = \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sum_{i \in C_j} \lVert x_i - \mu_j \rVert^2$$ where $\lVert \cdot \rVert$ is straight-line (Euclidean) distance. Because a centre is an average and distances are squared, $W$ is smallest for round groups of similar spread, and k-means tends to find groups of that shape. $W$ also falls every time $k$ rises, reaching zero when every point is its own group, so $W$ alone cannot say what $k$ should be. That is the subject of [the next page](choosing-the-number-of-clusters.qmd). ::: ## Worked example ### A community matrix holds 24 taxon counts per station This section adds a second table to the coastal survey: the same 800 stations, each with counts of 24 benthic taxa, `tax01` to `tax24`. It is simulated too, built on the survey's stations by `R/make-community-data.R`. One row per station and one column per taxon is the usual shape of a **community matrix**. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) tibble(stations = nrow(taxa_only), taxa = ncol(taxa_only), `zero counts (%)` = round(100 * mean(as.matrix(taxa_only) == 0)), `taxa per station (median)` = median(rowSums(taxa_only > 0)), `largest count` = max(taxa_only)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| stations| taxa| zero counts (%)| taxa per station (median)| largest count| |--------:|----:|---------------:|-------------------------:|-------------:| | 800| 24| 54| 11| 56|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") pd.DataFrame({ "stations": [len(taxa_only)], "taxa": [taxa_only.shape[1]], "zero counts (%)": [round(100 * (taxa_only == 0).to_numpy().mean())], "taxa per station (median)": [(taxa_only > 0).sum(axis=1).median()], "largest count": [taxa_only.to_numpy().max()], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | stations | taxa | zero counts (%) | taxa per station (median) | largest count | |-----------:|-------:|------------------:|----------------------------:|----------------:| | 800 | 24 | 54 | 11 | 56 | ::: ::: ::: The counts are like the survey's single species, only more so: 54% of them are zero, a typical station holds 11 of the 24 taxa, and a few counts are far larger than the rest. ### Counts are logged and standardised in a recipe Two steps prepare the counts, both from [Scaling and encoding](../02-marine-data/scaling-and-encoding.qmd). A log transform pulls in the few large counts, and standardising gives every taxon the same weight in the distance, so the commonest taxa do not decide the groups alone. `log(count + 1)` keeps the zeros at zero. The clustering itself comes from **tidyclust**, the tidymodels package for clustering. It keeps the shape used for every model so far: a recipe, a model specification, a workflow and a fit. The engine is R's own `kmeans()`, run from 25 random starts. This page sets $k$ to 2; [the next page](choosing-the-number-of-clusters.qmd) asks how to choose it. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cluster_recipe <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) kmeans_spec <- k_means(num_clusters = 2) |> set_engine("stats", nstart = 25, iter.max = 100) set.seed(41) habitat_fit <- workflow() |> add_recipe(cluster_recipe) |> add_model(kmeans_spec) |> fit(data = taxa_only) assignments <- extract_cluster_assignment(habitat_fit) count(assignments, .cluster) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|.cluster | n| |:---------|---:| |Cluster_1 | 183| |Cluster_2 | 617|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} from sklearn.cluster import KMeans from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler # step_log(offset = 1) then step_normalize. cluster_recipe = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ]) # n_init is nstart: 25 random starts, keeping the best. habitat_fit = Pipeline([ ("recipe", cluster_recipe), ("model", KMeans(n_clusters=2, n_init=25, max_iter=100, random_state=41)), ]).fit(taxa_only) # Number the clusters from 1, as tidyclust does. assignments = pd.Series(habitat_fit["model"].labels_ + 1, name="cluster") assignments.value_counts().sort_index().reset_index(name="n") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | cluster | n | |----------:|----:| | 1 | 183 | | 2 | 617 | ::: ::: ::: k-means returns two groups, of 617 and 183 stations. The cluster numbers are only labels, in whatever order the run found them. ### Two k-means clusters recover the hard and soft seabed k-means saw only the counts. The survey also recorded each station's seabed, so the clusters can be compared with something k-means never saw. Rock and gravel are **hard bottom**; sand and mud are **soft bottom**. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stations <- community |> mutate(cluster = assignments$.cluster) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "hard", "soft")) stations |> summarise(stations = n(), `hard bottom` = sum(bottom == "hard"), `soft bottom` = sum(bottom == "soft"), `median depth (m)` = round(median(depth_m)), `depth, 10th to 90th percentile (m)` = paste(round(quantile(depth_m, 0.1)), "to", round(quantile(depth_m, 0.9))), .by = cluster) |> arrange(cluster) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|cluster | stations| hard bottom| soft bottom| median depth (m)|depth, 10th to 90th percentile (m) | |:---------|--------:|-----------:|-----------:|----------------:|:----------------------------------| |Cluster_1 | 183| 181| 2| 66|27 to 132 | |Cluster_2 | 617| 13| 604| 96|42 to 148 |
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} stations = community.assign(cluster=assignments).merge( survey[["station_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id") stations["bottom"] = np.where(stations["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"]), "hard", "soft") (stations.groupby("cluster") .apply(lambda g: pd.Series({ "stations": len(g), "hard bottom": (g["bottom"] == "hard").sum(), "soft bottom": (g["bottom"] == "soft").sum(), "median depth (m)": round(g["depth_m"].median()), "depth, 10th to 90th percentile (m)": f"{round(g['depth_m'].quantile(0.1))} to " f"{round(g['depth_m'].quantile(0.9))}", }), include_groups=False) .reset_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | cluster | stations | hard bottom | soft bottom | median depth (m) | depth, 10th to 90th percentile (m) | |----------:|-----------:|--------------:|--------------:|-------------------:|:-------------------------------------| | 1 | 183 | 181 | 2 | 66 | 27 to 132 | | 2 | 617 | 13 | 604 | 96 | 42 to 148 | ::: ::: ::: One cluster is the hard bottom and the other the soft bottom: only 15 of the 800 stations sit in the other kind's cluster. From the counts alone, k-means has found the one real grouping built into the simulation, where six taxa live only on rock and gravel and eight only on sand and mud. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stations |> mutate(cluster = if_else(cluster == hard_cluster, "Hard-bottom cluster", "Soft-bottom cluster"), bottom = paste(str_to_sentence(bottom), "bottom")) |> ggplot(aes(depth_m, cluster, colour = bottom)) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.25, seed = 1), size = 1.4, alpha = 0.7) + labs(x = "depth (m)", y = NULL, colour = "recorded seabed") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Each station's depth and its cluster, coloured by the seabed the survey recorded. The clusters follow the seabed, not depth: each covers most of the depth range.](clustering_files/figure-html/fig-clusters-1.png){#fig-clusters fig-alt='A strip chart with depth in metres on the horizontal axis and the two clusters on the vertical axis, each station a jittered point coloured by hard or soft bottom. The hard-bottom cluster is almost all one colour and the soft-bottom cluster almost all the other, with 15 stations out of place. The hard-bottom cluster runs from about 27 to 132 metres for most of its stations and the soft-bottom cluster from about 42 to 148, so the two overlap over most of the shelf.' width=1500} ::: ::: ::: The clusters did not follow depth. The hard-bottom cluster is shallower on average, with a median of 66 m against 96 m, because rock and gravel lie shallower on this shelf, but most of its stations span 27 to 132 m and most of the other's 42 to 148 m. That does not make depth unimportant to these taxa. [Principal component analysis](principal-component-analysis.qmd) finds a strong depth pattern in the same counts. But species change with depth gradually, with no depth at which one set gives way to another, so there is no gap for k-means to split on. The seabed is a clean break between two kinds of ground. The difference between a group and a gradient runs through this section, up to [Checking a pattern before reporting it](interpreting-patterns.qmd). ## k-means returns groups in any table k-means always returns $k$ groups. Asked for four groups in points scattered at random, it returns four tidy ones, and nothing in its output says the groups are not really there; [Choosing the number of clusters](choosing-the-number-of-clusters.qmd) builds that check. It also gives every station a group, however far it sits from any centre. And its straight-line distance treats two stations that both lack a taxon as alike, which is why community ecologists often use other distances, such as Bray–Curtis. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - **Clustering** sorts rows into groups of similar rows, with no labels to learn from. - **k-means** repeats two steps, assign each point to its nearest centre and move each centre to the average of its points, and so lowers the **within-cluster sum of squares**. It is run from many random starts, and the best run is kept. - Distances need a common scale: log and standardise the counts in a recipe first. - On the community matrix, two clusters recovered the hard and soft seabed with 15 stations out of place, from counts alone. - They did not split by depth, which changes the species gradually, with no gap to split on. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Remove `step_normalize()` from `cluster_recipe` and refit. How many stations change cluster, and do the clusters still follow the seabed? 2. Fit k-means with `nstart = 1` under five different seeds and compare `extract_fit_engine(habitat_fit)$tot.withinss` across them. Do the runs all end at the same sum of squares?
